extraction_notes.note: Blueprint restates textbook graph notions and folklore BFS correctness with no citation; marked origin external ('standard (uncited)') per Hard rule 3, with the proofs as paper. No main results marked: there is no abstract or introduction.
Most sections (Trees, Coloring, Matching, Shortest Path, Union Find, ...) are empty headings in this blueprint; nothing to extract. 'Walk' is used throughout but never defined.

nodes.name: Undirected graph
nodes.statement: An \textit{(undirected) graph} is a pair $G = (V,E)$ consisting of a set $V$ and a multi-set $E$ of unordered pairs of elements in $V$. Elements of $V$ are called \textit{vertices} and elements of $E$ are called \textit{edges}. For two vertices $u,v \in V$, we say $u$ and $v$ are \textit{adjacent} if $\{u,v\} \in E$. We call an undirected graph $G$ \textit{simple} if all edges are distinct (i.e., $E$ is a set), and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.
differentia: consisting of a set $V$ and a multi-set $E$ of unordered pairs of elements in $V$
nodes.statement_short: Undirected multigraph $(V,E)$ with vertices, edges, adjacency, and simple graphs (no repeated edges or loops).

nodes.name: Directed graph
nodes.statement: A \textit{directed graph} is a pair $G = (V,E)$ consisting of a set $V$ and a multi-set $E$ of ordered pairs of elements in $V$. Elements of $V$ are called \textit{vertices} and elements of $E$ are called \textit{edges}. We call a directed graph $G$ \textit{simple} if all edges are distinct and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.
differentia: consisting of a set $V$ and a multi-set $E$ of ordered pairs of elements in $V$
nodes.statement_short: Directed multigraph with ordered-pair edges; simple if edges are distinct and loop-free.

nodes.name: Reachability
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a simple graph or a simple directed graph. A vertex $v$ is \emph{reachable} from $u$ if some walk realized in $G$ runs from $u$ to $v$. In the undirected case reachability is an equivalence relation on $\V{G}$; in the directed case it is only a preorder, since walks cannot be reversed.
differentia: some walk realized in $G$ runs from $u$ to $v$
nodes.statement_short: $v$ is reachable from $u$ if a walk in $G$ goes from $u$ to $v$; an equivalence relation (undirected) or preorder (directed).
nodes.label: def:reachable-directed

nodes.name: Symmetric orientation
nodes.statement: The \emph{symmetric orientation} of a simple graph $G$ is the simple directed graph on $\V{G}$ whose arcs are the ordered pairs $(u, v)$ with $\{u, v\} \in \E{G}$. A walk is realized in $G$ exactly when it is realized in the symmetric orientation, so reachability and distances agree.
differentia: whose arcs are the ordered pairs $(u, v)$ with $\{u, v\} \in \E{G}$
nodes.statement_short: Directed graph with both arcs $(u,v),(v,u)$ for each undirected edge; preserves walks, reachability and distances.
nodes.label: def:symmetric-orientation

nodes.name: Distance
nodes.statement: The \emph{distance} $\dist(u, v) \in \N \cup \{\infty\}$ from $u$ to $v$ in a simple directed graph is the least length of a walk from $u$ to $v$, and $\infty$ if $v$ is not reachable from $u$. For a simple graph it is the distance in the symmetric orientation, and is then symmetric in $u$ and $v$.
differentia: the least length of a walk from $u$ to $v$, and $\infty$ if $v$ is not reachable from $u$
nodes.statement_short: Graph distance: least walk length from $u$ to $v$, $\infty$ if unreachable; via symmetric orientation for undirected graphs.
nodes.label: def:dist

nodes.name: BFS layers
nodes.statement: Let $s \in \V{G}$. The \emph{layers} of breadth-first search from $s$ are the sets \[ L_0 = \{s\}, \qquad L_{k+1} = N^+(L_k) \setminus (L_0 \cup \dots \cup L_k), \] where $N^+(L)$ denotes the set of out-neighbours of the vertices of $L$. The set of vertices \emph{visited} within $k$ rounds is $V_k = L_0 \cup \dots \cup L_k$. When $s \notin \V{G}$ every layer is empty. In Lean the search is a state $(V_k, L_k)$ iterated $k$ times from $(\{s\}, \{s\})$, so that the definition reduces and \texttt{decide} can evaluate it.
nodes.statement_short: BFS layers $L_k$: $L_0=\{s\}$, $L_{k+1}$ = new out-neighbours of $L_k$; $V_k$ = vertices visited within $k$ rounds.
nodes.label: def:bfs-layers

nodes.name: Soundness of BFS layers
nodes.statement: Every vertex of $L_k$ is the endpoint of a walk of length $k$ from $s$.
conclusions: Every vertex of $L_k$ is the endpoint of a walk of length $k$ from $s$.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-sound

nodes.name: Proof of Soundness
nodes.statement: By induction on $k$: a vertex of $L_{k+1}$ is an out-neighbour of a vertex of $L_k$, and appending that arc to the walk given by the induction hypothesis yields a walk of length $k + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: extend the walk to a vertex of $L_k$ by the arc to its out-neighbour in $L_{k+1}$.

nodes.name: Completeness of BFS layers
nodes.statement: The endpoint of a walk of length $\ell$ from $s$ lies in $V_\ell$.
conclusions: The endpoint of a walk of length $\ell$ from $s$ lies in $V_\ell$.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-complete

nodes.name: Proof of Completeness
nodes.statement: By induction on the walk. The key step is that the out-neighbours of a vertex of $V_k$ lie in $V_{k+1}$: such a vertex lies in some $L_j$ with $j \le k$, and its out-neighbours are either already in $V_j$ or in $L_{j+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the walk; key step: out-neighbours of a vertex of $V_k$ lie in $V_{k+1}$.

nodes.name: Termination of BFS
nodes.statement: If $L_k \neq \emptyset$ then $k < |\V{G}|$. Hence the search from $s$ has exhausted every layer after $|\V{G}|$ rounds.
conclusions: the search from $s$ has exhausted every layer after $|\V{G}|$ rounds
nodes.statement_short: A nonempty layer has index below $|V(G)|$, so BFS finishes within $|V(G)|$ rounds.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-termination

nodes.name: Proof of Termination
nodes.statement: An empty layer is followed by an empty layer, so $L_0, \dots, L_k$ are all non-empty. They are pairwise disjoint subsets of $\V{G}$, so $k + 1 \le |V_k| \le |\V{G}|$.
nodes.statement_short: Counting: layers up to $k$ are nonempty and pairwise disjoint subsets of $V(G)$, so $k+1 \le |V(G)|$.

nodes.name: The layers are the spheres
nodes.statement: For every vertex $v$ and every $k \in \N$, \[ v \in L_k \iff \dist(s, v) = k . \]
nodes.statement_short: BFS layer $L_k$ is exactly the sphere of radius $k$ around $s$.
nodes.label: thm:bfs-layers-spheres

nodes.name: Proof that the layers are the spheres
nodes.statement: Let $v \in L_k$. Soundness gives $\dist(s, v) \le k$. For the reverse inequality there is nothing to show when $k = 0$; when $k = j + 1$, a walk from $s$ to $v$ of length at most $j$ would place $v$ in $V_j$ by completeness, whereas $L_{j+1}$ avoids $V_j$ by construction, so $\dist(s, v) > j$, i.e. $\dist(s, v) \ge k$. Conversely, if $\dist(s, v) = k$ then a shortest walk places $v \in V_k$, so $v \in L_j$ for some $j \le k$, and the first part gives $j = k$.
nodes.statement_short: Soundness gives $\dist \le k$, completeness plus disjointness of $L_{j+1}$ from $V_j$ gives $\dist \ge k$; converse via a shortest walk.

nodes.name: BFS computes reachability and distance
nodes.statement: The set $V_{|\V{G}|}$ is exactly the set of vertices reachable from $s$, and the least $k < |\V{G}|$ with $v \in L_k$ (or $\infty$ if there is none) is exactly $\dist(s, v)$.
conclusions: The set $V_{|\V{G}|}$ is exactly the set of vertices reachable from $s$
the least $k < |\V{G}|$ with $v \in L_k$ (or $\infty$ if there is none) is exactly $\dist(s, v)$
nodes.statement_short: After $|V(G)|$ rounds BFS has visited exactly the reachable vertices, and the first layer containing $v$ gives $\dist(s,v)$.
nodes.label: thm:bfs-correct

nodes.name: Proof of BFS correctness
nodes.statement: Soundness gives one inclusion and one inequality; completeness together with the termination bound gives the other.
nodes.statement_short: Combine soundness for one inclusion/inequality with completeness and the termination bound for the other.

nodes.name: Standing assumption on the searched graph
nodes.statement: Throughout, $G$ is a simple directed graph whose vertex set $\V{G}$ is finite and given as data, and whose arc membership is decidable.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ is a simple directed graph with finite vertex set given as data and decidable arcs.

nodes.name: Undirected search via symmetric orientation
nodes.statement: Undirected graphs are searched through their symmetric orientation (Definition~\ref{def:symmetric-orientation}), so one search serves both kinds of graph.

nodes.name: Upper bound by soundness
nodes.statement: Let $v \in L_k$. Soundness gives $\dist(s, v) \le k$.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: For the reverse inequality there is nothing to show when $k = 0$; when $k = j + 1$, a walk from $s$ to $v$ of length at most $j$ would place $v$ in $V_j$ by completeness, whereas $L_{j+1}$ avoids $V_j$ by construction, so $\dist(s, v) > j$, i.e. $\dist(s, v) \ge k$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound: trivial for $k=0$; for $k=j+1$ completeness and disjointness from $V_j$ give $\dist > j$.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $\dist(s, v) = k$ then a shortest walk places $v \in V_k$, so $v \in L_j$ for some $j \le k$, and the first part gives $j = k$.
nodes.statement_short: Converse: a shortest walk puts $v$ in some $L_j$, $j \le k$, and the first part forces $j=k$.
